overview: The file consists chiefly of three American diplomatic reports on the October 1930 Wushe uprising in Japanese-ruled Taiwan, describing the massacre of Japanese residents, the Indigenous rebels’ grievances, and the subsequent military and police campaign. The reports discuss wage discrimination, compulsory labor, sexual misconduct by Japanese policemen, earlier disarmament and repression, headhunting, censorship, air power, rumored poison-gas use, and suspicions that Japanese forces executed women and children while reporting their deaths as suicides. They also trace the political repercussions within the Taiwan Government-General, Japanese military leadership, the Imperial Diet, and the Seiyūkai Party. A final, apparently unrelated 1935 Department of State memorandum concerns a Fourth of July reception given by the American consul at Taihoku and complaints about diplomatic dress in the summer heat.

subfiles.title: Forbes despatch on the outbreak of the Wushe uprising
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the outbreak, possible causes, and initial Japanese suppression of an Indigenous uprising in central Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports a major Indigenous uprising in Taiwan killed many Japanese, suspecting police mistreatment of Indigenous women as a root grievance.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 53 on features of the Wushe uprising
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese aerial operations, censorship, rumored poison-gas use, possible grievances, and the rebels’ deliberate targeting of Japanese people.
subfiles.summary: Young reports Japanese aircraft bombed the Wushe rebels amid censored poison-gas rumors, and that Chinese residents were spared, showing the revolt targeted Japanese specifically.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 58 on the causes, suppression, and political consequences of the Wushe uprising
subfiles.from: Charles S. Reed II, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Provides an extensive review of the uprising’s causes, course, suppression, alleged atrocities, and repercussions in Japanese colonial and metropolitan politics.
subfiles.summary: Reed attributes the organized uprising to accumulated grievances that included wage discrimination, coerced labor in lieu of taxes, sexual misconduct and broken marriages, culturally insensitive policing, earlier harsh subjugation, and the confiscation of Indigenous rifles. He discusses political repercussions for Taiwan officials and the Tokyo government, as well as a public dispute between Generals Hishikari and Watanabe over troop deployment and military efficiency. The report identifies ten participating villages, estimates 372 active rebels from a population of 1,552, and states that approximately 70 percent of Musha’s Japanese population was killed before troops, police, artillery, and aircraft largely suppressed the revolt within twenty days. Reed records but cannot verify rumors of poison-gas bombing and suspicions that Japanese forces executed Indigenous men, women, and children whose deaths were officially presented as suicides; he concludes that the colonial administration nevertheless intended to continue its existing policy with only limited labor reforms.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on the Taihoku Fourth of July reception
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Comments on an attached but absent consular despatch describing a Fourth of July reception at Taihoku and the discomfort of American diplomatic dress.
subfiles.summary: Memo describes a successful consular Fourth of July reception, and a bill on Foreign Service dress abroad.

interest: Shows the 1930 Wushe uprising in Taiwan, including censored reports of chemical warfare and suspected mass executions.
